entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Philocles was an Athenian general whose command during the final, desperate phase of the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) proved catastrophic for Athens. His name is inextricably linked with the disastrous Battle of Aegospotami in 405 BCE, a pivotal engagement that irrevocably sealed Athens' defeat against the Spartan-led Peloponnesian League. His actions, or inactions, at this critical juncture led directly to the end of Athenian naval supremacy, the collapse of its empire, and the profound transformation of the Greek world, marking the definitive conclusion of Athens' Golden Age.

Prior to Aegospotami, Philocles served in various military capacities during the Ionian War, the final stage of the Peloponnesian conflict. His most defining moment arrived in 405 BCE when he was one of the six Athenian strategoi commanding the main Athenian fleet, comprising approximately 180 triremes, stationed near the Hellespont, close to the Spartan-held Lampsacus. Despite repeated warnings, including one famously attributed to the exiled Alcibiades, Philocles and his fellow generals, notably Conon and Adeimantus, allowed their fleet to be caught unprepared and vulnerable by the cunning Spartan admiral Lysander. The ensuing rout resulted in the capture or destruction of 160 out of 180 Athenian triremes and the brutal massacre of some 3,000 Athenian sailors and generals, including Philocles himself, who was executed by Lysander.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Philocles' command at the Battle of Aegospotami in 405 BCE directly contributed to the destruction of the Athenian fleet, leading to Athens' surrender and the end of the Peloponnesian War. This event irrevocably altered the balance of power in the Aegean and marked the demise of the Athenian Empire.
